A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same safe-bidding research by Golrezaei and Sahoo. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison, including matching proofs and experiments across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5.3, Figure 4, and Appendix E report original simulations using reconstructed EU ETS auction data, averaged over 100 simulations.

after.justification: V3 retains the original simulations and adds experiments evaluating shifted safe strategies under cumulative RoI constraints in Section 6.2, Figure 5, and Table 2.

M1.justification: The core safe-strategy and DAG framework remains, but Algorithm 1 changes its initialization to sample initial paths uniformly. Section 6 and Appendix E introduce substantive adaptations: covering-path exploration with biased estimates for adaptive adversaries, surplus-dependent shifted bids for cumulative RoI, and separate contextual learners for stochastic and adversarial valuations.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same reconstructed 2022–2023 EU ETS auction data. V3 adds evaluation under sliding-window RoI requirements, allowing individual-round violations. This expands the tested financial-constraint scenario within the retained auction domain; adaptive competitors and changing valuations receive theoretical treatment rather than empirical evaluation.

E2.justification: The strategy-class comparisons in Figure 4 remain. The new Figure 5 additionally evaluates shifted safe bidding against the unshifted online safe-bidding algorithm with per-round constraints, T0 = 1. This introduces a concrete online reference comparison without adding evaluated external bidding algorithms.

E3.justification: V3 adds an online evaluation design measuring cumulative-value gains and per-round financial feasibility, beyond v2's offline richness-ratio experiments. Section 6.2 sets T = 200, tests T0 = 1, 8, 16, 50, and infinity, and fixes m = 4 for feasibility measurements. It introduces relative-gain and relative-feasibility metrics. Separately, Figure 4 switches from Lambda to its reciprocal alpha while retaining its original sampling settings.

E4.justification: Section 6.2 adds a focused sensitivity analysis of RoI-window length and bid expressiveness, including the distribution of per-round feasibility and violation frequencies. It tests how relaxing the financial constraint affects value and risk. The existing richness-ratio analysis remains substantively intact.

E5.justification: V3 explicitly identifies Figure 4's shaded regions as one standard deviation; v2 shows shading without defining it. Both retain 100 simulations for that experiment. V3 separately reports 50 simulations for each new Section 6.2 experiment, without establishing any increase in repetitions of the original experiment.

E6.justification: V3 adds substantive online value-and-risk results in Figure 5 and Table 2. For m = 4, it reports approximately 21% higher cumulative value at T0 = infinity alongside a 0.4235 per-round violation fraction; T0 = 8 gives approximately 10% higher value and a 0.3225 violation fraction. These comparisons relax the constraint. Original Figure 4 findings remain consistent under reciprocal reporting, including approximately 1.25 becoming 0.8.

T1.justification: Section 6 and Appendix E add adaptive-adversary regret guarantees, a cumulative-RoI impossibility theorem under Assumption 6.4, and contextual regret upper and lower bounds. Appendix B also adds a uniform-initial-path proof and derives O(mM^2) bandit marginal computation instead of v2's stated O(mM^3). The principal safe-strategy characterizations and richness bounds remain; much of the relocated Section 5.4 proof already existed in v2.

C1.justification: V3's abstract, contributions, and conclusion extend the paper's claimed scope to adaptive competitors, cumulative RoI, and time-varying valuations. V2 explicitly listed cumulative RoI and changing valuations as future work. The central safe-strategy, efficient-learning, and richness-ratio claims are retained, with new claims of adaptability supported by the added extensions.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive interpretation of the value-versus-feasibility trade-off and guidance for choosing RoI windows according to risk preferences. It explains why the partial feedback is technically semi-bandit feedback and how this supports its regret guarantees. It also makes applicability boundaries more explicit through the oblivious/adaptive distinction, the cumulative-RoI impossibility assumption, and finite-context, full-information valuation extensions.

D1.justification: V3 supplies explicit forward/backward recurrences for bandit marginal probabilities, covering-path construction and parameter choices for the adaptive algorithm, and contextual memory and update requirements. Section 6.2 specifies positive competing bids and the zero-payment convention for relative feasibility. The original data-reconstruction procedure, tolerance, retained auction count, and Figure 4 simulation settings remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially, including a new Data-Driven Methods in Auctions discussion covering reserve-price optimization, boosting, and learned auction design. V3 also adds contextual-learning, adaptive-adversary, and semi-bandit connections, including Balseiro et al. (2019) and Gyorgy et al. (2007). These additions broaden the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract, contribution narrative, learning-algorithm explanation, and conclusion. It adds Managerial Insights and a front table of contents, brings existing proofs and bandit material into the main text, and reorganizes the appendices around the new extensions. These are substantial changes to exposition and document structure.

P2.justification: Figure 4 is redrawn with reciprocal axes, explicit worst-case curves, legends, and a clarified caption. V3 adds Figure 5's gain curves and feasibility box plots plus the empirical Table 2. It also redraws the DAG, combines the original learning and update pseudocode, adds extension algorithms, and relocates the existing m = 1 lower-bound table into the main text.

improvement.justification: V3 improves exposition and computational detail and develops modeling questions that v2 left open. However, the new sliding-window feasibility guarantee has an unresolved gap: Eq. (24) can produce a negative shift when earlier surplus leaves the window, whereas the shifted strategy class and the stated violation bound require a nonnegative shift. The PDF does not address this case. The useful extensions and clearer presentation therefore coexist with an unsupported guarantee in a highlighted practical contribution, preventing a reliable net-quality judgment.
